changes.before: The **representativeness heuristic** is judging how likely something is by **how much it resembles a typical case**. The probability that A belongs to class B is judged by how well A's properties match the properties normally associated with class B. >> We ask whether something looks like a typical member of a category. || America has **far more farms than libraries**. A randomly picked man named Robert wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, and the question is whether he is more likely a librarian or a farmer. >> Most people say librarian, because the description fits the stereotype. >> They **ignore the base rate**, the fact that there are so many more farmers than librarians.
changes.after: The **representativeness heuristic** is judging how likely something is by **how much it resembles a typical case**. The probability that A belongs to class B is judged by how well A's properties match the properties normally associated with class B. >> We ask whether something looks like a typical member of a category. || America has **far more farms than libraries**. A randomly picked man named Robert wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, and the question is whether he is more likely a librarian or a farmer. >> Most people say librarian, because the description fits the stereotype. >> **Base rates** describe how common the occupations are, but counts of farms and libraries alone do not establish how many farmers or librarians there are.

changes.before: **Lord and coworkers** had people who supported capital punishment and people who opposed it read the same article. Those in favor found that the article supported their view, and those against found that it supported theirs. >> The same evidence pushed each group further toward what it already believed. || This is the **myside bias**, the tendency to generate and evaluate evidence and test hypotheses in a way that is biased toward our own opinions and attitudes. People focused on information that agreed with their beliefs and disregarded information that did not. >> Each side read the article through the lens of its own position.

changes.before: In this dilemma, a convoy of food trucks is headed to a refugee camp during a famine, and a second camp turns out to have many more refugees. Sending the convoy to the second camp would save the many people there, but the smaller group in the first camp would die as a result. >> The question is whether to send the convoy to the second camp. || By expected utility, rerouting is clearly better, because it saves far more lives than it costs. Yet **Ritov and Baron** found that **most people did not choose to reroute the convoy**. >> Some people said they would not reroute it even if only one person in the first camp would die, so the act of causing deaths outweighed the lives saved.
changes.after: In this dilemma, a convoy of food trucks is headed to a refugee camp during a famine, and a second camp turns out to have many more refugees. changes.before: **Tetlock and colleagues** proposed the **sacred value protection model**, which says that **people want to protect what they hold sacred**. Sacred values are kept in a separate compartment from ordinary, everyday values. >> Things like a human life are treated as different in kind from money. || When the two kinds of values are mixed together, people feel threatened and respond with **moral outrage**, which is called a **taboo** tradeoff. When two sacred values are weighed against each other, people are much less outraged, which is called a **tragic** tradeoff. >> Comparing a life with money feels wrong, while comparing one life with another feels sad but acceptable.
changes.after: **Tetlock and colleagues (2000)** proposed the **sacred value protection model**, which says that **people want to protect what they hold sacred**. Sacred values are kept in a separate compartment from ordinary, everyday values. >> Things like a human life are treated as different in kind from money. || When the two kinds of values are mixed together, people feel threatened and respond with **moral outrage**, which is called a **taboo** tradeoff. When two sacred values are weighed against each other, people are much less outraged, which is called a **tragic** tradeoff. >> Comparing a life with money feels wrong, while comparing one life with another feels sad but acceptable.
reasons: Restore the researcher and year naturally while preserving the Version 21 explanation.

changes.before: In the **taboo tradeoff scenario**, a hospital administrator can save a young boy who needs a liver transplant, but the transplant would cost the hospital a million dollars that could be spent on other needs. The choice sets a child's life against money. >> That mixes a sacred value with an ordinary one. || In the **tragic tradeoff scenario**, two children need a liver transplant, but there is only one liver. Here a sacred value is weighed against another sacred value, and there is no way to avoid losing one.
changes.after: In the **taboo tradeoff scenario** used by **Tetlock and colleagues (2000)**, a hospital administrator can save a young boy who needs a liver transplant, but the transplant would cost the hospital a million dollars that could be spent on other needs. changes.before: In the **taboo** case, people were extremely outraged when the administrator **did not save the boy**, and much less outraged when he did. Choosing between two lives was seen as painful but not as a betrayal of sacred values.

changes.before: The **framing effect** is when the way a choice is worded changes the decision. The wording can point people toward what they might gain or what they might lose. >> The outcomes themselves can stay exactly the same. || **Tversky and Kahneman** found that when a choice is framed as gains, people play it safe and take the sure thing. When the same choice is framed as losses, people take the gamble instead. >> Wording alone can flip someone from avoiding risk to seeking it.
changes.after: The **framing effect** is when the way a choice is worded changes the decision. The wording can point people toward what they might gain or what they might lose. >> The outcomes themselves can stay exactly the same. || **Tversky and Kahneman (1981)** found that when a choice is framed as gains, people play it safe and take the sure thing. When the same choice is framed as losses, people take the gamble instead. >> Wording alone can flip someone from avoiding risk to seeking it.
reasons: Retain Version 20/21 spelling Kahneman; the original source has the extra-n spelling Kahnemann. Restore the printed year.

changes.before: A disease is expected to kill six hundred people, and two programs are described in terms of lives saved. One program saves two hundred people for sure, while the other has a one in three chance of saving everyone and a two in three chance of saving no one. >> This is the gain frame. || Most people, about seven in ten, chose the sure thing. They locked in two hundred lives rather than risk saving no one. >> In a gain frame, people avoid risk.
changes.after: In the gain frame studied by **Tversky and Kahneman (1981)**, a disease is expected to kill six hundred people, and two programs are described in terms of lives saved. One program saves two hundred people for sure, while the other has a one in three chance of saving everyone and a two in three chance of saving no one. >> This is the gain frame. || Most people, about seven in ten, chose the sure thing. They locked in two hundred lives rather than risk saving no one. >> In a gain frame, people avoid risk.
reasons: Pages 11–12 continue the framing study introduced on source page 9. Attribute the same experiment without claiming a separate study.

changes.before: Now the same choice is described in terms of deaths. The sure option is identical to before, since saving two hundred of six hundred means four hundred die, so only the wording changed. >> That reversal is the framing effect.
changes.after: In the loss frame studied by **Tversky and Kahneman (1981)**, the same choice is described in terms of deaths. One program means four hundred people die for sure, while the other has a one in three chance that no one dies and a two in three chance that everyone dies. >> This is the loss frame. || This time most people, about four in five, chose the gamble. changes.before: **Sanfey and coworkers** used the **ultimatum game**, in which a proposer gets ten dollars and offers the responder some way to split it. The responder can accept the split or reject it, and if the responder rejects it, neither player gets anything. >> A rejection costs both players. || According to utility theory, the rational decision for the responder is to accept any offer at all. Even a single dollar is worth more than the nothing that comes from rejecting. >> A purely rational responder would never turn down free money.
changes.after: **Sanfey and colleagues (2003)** used the **ultimatum game**, in which a proposer gets ten dollars and offers the responder some way to split it. The responder can accept the split or reject it, and if the responder rejects it, neither player gets anything. >> A rejection costs both players. || If the responder aims only to maximize the money received, accepting any positive offer is better than rejecting it. Even a single dollar is worth more money than the nothing that comes from rejecting. >> This monetary prediction treats a positive offer as better than no payment.
reasons: Restore the researcher and year naturally while preserving the Version 21 explanation.
